newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Bank competition impact not fully seen - RBA.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Bank competition impact not fully seen - RBA.

text.p: The breakdown of the traditional structure of the Australian banking market has placed increasing pressure on bank profits, and the full impact has yet to be seen, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) research has found.
Developments in information technology have transformed the cost structure of the finance industry, and led to increasing competition and the emergence of specialised product lines.

"Many of these developments are still at a relatively early stage and are likely to have important ongoing consequences for the finance industry as they are worked out more fully," Malcolm Edey, Head of Economic Research, said in a report.
"The full impact of the new competitive pressures on bank profits is yet to be seen," he said in the RBA paper, "The Future of the Financial System".
Technology had transformed cost structures and made available new products and delivery systems, as well as reducing entry costs, particularly for specialised products.

"This in turn has increased the contestability of markets for a number of products, as has been illustrated recently by the growing competition from new players in the home mortgage market," Edey said.
There was a widespread perception that financial sector change was set to continue, with the U.S. seen as the leader.

Edey said there was now debate in the U.S. about the future of traditional banking. While they had been able to compete in new areas such as securitised lending and other fee based activities, bank assets as a proportion of the U.S. financial system have experienced a long term decline.
The RBA found that locally there was little evidence, at an aggregate level, of that sort of decline in traditional banking.

Since deregulation, banks had significantly recovered market share on a total asset basis, with profits recovering to high levels after being hit by major increase in loan write-offs in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Edey said.

In simplified terms, traditional banking was the joint provision of deposit, loan and transaction services, with the bank's competitive position supported by a an extensive branch network and access to low cost deposits, Edey said.
There was limited competition outside the group of full-service providers, and pricing was based mainly on the net interest margins with very low fees for transaction services.

"A significant challenge to this market structure has come from the emergence of much stronger competition on a product by product basis, stimulated by specialist suppliers of individual product lines," Edey said.

Examples included cash management trusts on the deposit side, and mortgage originators on the lending side, with the common thread being the ability to offer deposit and loan products on a stand alone basis at competitive prices.
This placed pressure on banks to price their key products on a similar basis.
In turn, this saw the interest margins compressed, placing pressure on banks to cut costs and reduce cross subsidisation of transaction services.
Edey said lower market entry costs, and the ability to offer specialised products, will see a re-examination of cost structures, and place further pressure on cross-subsidisation.
While this do not necessarily mean a diminishing role for banks, it did imply an increased potential for the nature on banking business to change, Edey said.
